claims.text: Equiatomic NbMoTaW has a single-phase BCC structure.
Equiatomic NbMoTaW has excellent mechanical strength at 1600 °C.
Equiatomic NbMoTaW has very poor room-temperature ductility.
Adding approximately 0.5 at% Hf and applying the proposed heat treatment will precipitate Hf-rich particles in NbMoTaW.
The Hf-rich precipitates will be nanoscale, coherent, and finely dispersed at grain and phase boundaries in a BCC NbMoTaW matrix.
Solutionizing at approximately 1400 °C for 20 minutes is suitable for establishing the desired precursor microstructure.
Aging at approximately 600 °C for 120 hours will promote controlled Hf-rich nanoprecipitation in NbMoTaW.
Vacuum arc melting or a comparable high-temperature production method will ensure chemical homogeneity.
Hf-rich precipitates will locally relieve stress concentrations.
Hf-rich precipitates will provide additional dislocation sources and facilitate dislocation activation and mobility at room temperature.
The enhanced dislocation activity will significantly improve room-temperature tensile ductility.
Fine coherent Hf-rich precipitates will pin dislocations at high temperature and preserve the 1600 °C yield strength.
The Hf-modified alloy will retain high-temperature mechanical performance comparable to untreated NbMoTaW at 1600 °C.
The Hf-rich precipitates will not act as sites for radiation-induced defect clustering.
The Hf-modified alloy will retain irradiation resistance similar to untreated NbMoTaW.
The beneficial effects require Hf to remain near the trace level of 0.5 at% and the precipitates to remain fine and coherent.
Excess Hf or uncontrolled heat treatment may form coarse or brittle intermetallics that degrade high-temperature performance or irradiation stability.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts significantly improved room-temperature ductility, whereas the cited Hf-alloy study reports that room-temperature performance remained almost unchanged. That study also concerns a different Al-Cr-Fe-Ni-Mo alloy system.
